results.title: Personal Computing 2.0: It's time for a personal computing revolution
results.author: Josh Albrecht
results.content:
In halcyon days of yore (circa 1995), computers always did what you told them. They were a delight to use. Ever since I was a kid and my parents brought home our first Mac, I’ve loved personal computing and the idea that I could create anything I could imagine.
There were no subscriptions, no login screens, no cookie banners, no notifications, no pop-ups, no up-sells, no ads, no rage-bait, and none of the crap to which we have grudgingly grown accustomed.
But Personal Computing 1.0 was far from perfect. It was clunky. It was under-powered. Your computer couldn’t really talk to my computer (except by literally calling on the phone and making noises at each other). Information had to be accessed by finding the right floppy disk for the correct Encyclopedia Britannica volume.
Then The Internet happened.
Suddenly, all of humanity’s collective knowledge was available at our fingertips. There were thousands--then millions--of incredible personal websites and blogs and new fun crazy experiments. A billion flowers bloomed.
But over time, those blooms became surrounded by noxious weeds. The ever-grasping slime-mold-that-is-Moloch reached its enshittifying tendrils around the roots of the web, slowly strangling it. Bit by bit, abandoned personal blog after dead side project, Big Tech shed its “Do No Evil” skin and relentlessly “improved” the “efficiency” of our shared digital commons. Spammy listicles and product pages replaced “unmonetized” information in search results, and social networks shifted from “creating connection” to manufacturing addicts.
In a sense, this transition culminated with the rise of closed AI. These companies illegally acquired practically ~every book ever written and got off with a slap on the wrist (unlike Aaron Swartz, who stole far less and then actually died). They scraped all of the collective wisdom of the web (from Wikipedia, Stack Overflow, Reddit, Arxiv, etc), and now sell it back to us and while simultaneously arguing for laws to prevent anyone else from doing the same. The net effect of all of this? A “dead internet“ filled with endless AI slop--slop writing, slop images, slop music, and security-vulnerability-ridden slop code.
But history repeats itself.
Much like the mainframe computing era gave birth to desktop computing 1.0 as processors and memory became faster and cheaper, so too could today’s closed AI labs give birth to an era of ubiquitous, smaller, open models. Everyone could have access to effectively unlimited intelligence and productive capability, and for marginally more than the cost of the electricity.
The dawn of Personal Computing 2.0
In my vision for this future, Personal Computing 2.0 is a computing paradigm that appropriately places AI (and all technology) as subservient to human concerns since, after all, the purpose of technology is to make our lives better.
Like Personal Computing 1.0, Personal Computing 2.0 puts the individual user at the center of the technological system. Personal Computing 2.0 is about making the interfaces and software environments that empower people to do their life’s work. It’s about unleashing the creative potential of individuals.
To accomplish this, Personal Computing 2.0’s central principle is that your data is yours. From this, everything else follows.
Your computing environment should belong to you
The revolution begins with liberating your data. Instead of having your data “live in the cloud”, i.e. where some company can force you into a subscription plan to access your old files or remove API access to your own data, Personal Computing 2.0 is about giving you full ownership over your data. You can use it however you want. You can take it anywhere you want.
Personal Computing 2.0 is a recognition that computing has become a central part of our lives. Losing my access to my Mac as a kid would have been sad, but ultimately forgotten. That is no longer the case: getting locked out of your Apple or Google account can mean losing access to most of your personal information, your photos, and even your personal memories. And being cut off from computing completely is almost unthinkable--many of us wouldn’t be able to work or live without access to any computing devices. The ability to delete your life and career is far more power than any one company should have.
That principle of ownership has a few important consequences.
Personal Computing 2.0 must be cross-platform. It’s inherently multi-vendor. Just like you could use Microsoft Paint and Adobe Photoshop on your Windows PC, so too should you be able to use Claude and Muse and Dot, together on your computer. They should be able to talk to each other. You should be able to script them. You should be able to use them from whatever interface(s) you want. Personal Computing should work on your literal laptop, or on any computer--that abandoned desktop in your closet, a Raspberry Pi, your old Xbox, and yes, even a computer that you’re renting from a cloud provider. And you should be able to instantly migrate between any of these providers (e.g, if someone tries to jack up the price on you!)
One of the beautiful things about Personal Computing 2.0 is that, as much as these companies might not want it to be so, the genie is out of the bottle: open-weight AI models are nearly good enough that a model running on your laptop can use even their closed agents for you (by controlling your browser or creating a program to run on your phone). Not only does this enable the seamless migration from one computer to another, but it puts these “closed AI platform agents” squarely where they should be: in competition with one another. We want to avoid the platform-effects and other anti-competitive dynamics that contributed to the decline of the web, which means forcing these new AI companies to compete on cost, performance, and reliability--not on finding ingenious new ways of locking us in and “generating shareholder value” by extracting it from us.
Personal Computing 2.0 is naturally a more privacy-preserving way of relating to computing. The privacy concerns of the past two decades are largely caused by the shift in where our data lived. There were no real privacy concerns in Personal Computing 1.0 because it was obvious where your data lived: on your computer. You obviously controlled that. And by taking advantage of advances in encryption and cloud storage, Personal Computing 2.0 returns us to a world where the data is fully under your control and effectively solves most of the privacy concerns that have plagued us for the past decade.
Your computer should adapt to you
But ownership isn’t only valuable because it gives us more control and privacy. Bringing all of your data together also enables entirely new kinds of computing.
The olds among us will remember when Google Desktop existed (and was useful). For a brief moment in time, you could literally find anything, instantly. It was an incredible feeling, and an incredible product. The only reason it died was that--as the Internet increasingly became the center of gravity for our data--it just made less sense. It ceased to have access to all of our data, which made it progressively less useful until it eventually died. Today, we struggle to find and use the data that is scattered across our dozens of SaaS subscriptions.
But Personal Computing 2.0 changes this.
When all of your data is yours--when it’s fully under your control--it becomes possible to find things again. To breathe more easily. To feel more relaxed. To be less scattered. As this happens, we may start to wonder:
- what do I actually want to do with this data?
- what do I want to build?
- what do I want my digital life to look like?
Personal Computing 2.0 is about discovering the answers to these questions together.
Personal Computing 2.0 is personal. We all have different answers to these questions. That’s part of the point! Just as we customize our home decor and our physical work spaces, we want everyone to be free to create whole new, personalized interfaces and systems and programs.
And today, we’re much better equipped to make those systems than we were during the first era of personal computing.
We now have access to a kind of computing power that simply wasn’t available back then. This is partly about faster processors and more memory, but it’s also about serverless compute: the ability to get 1,000 computers working for you for one second, rather than having to wait 1,000 seconds for your computer to do that same work. This enables applications that otherwise have required a massive cloud server and some SaaS app, and which we no longer need. But the computing power we have now is also different in the kind of compute that we can do: AI empowers anyone to make a computer do what they want in a way that was previously only accessible to professional computer engineers. AI unlocks a mode of interaction with our computers that was previously in the realm of science fiction: being able to talk to your computer, and have it understand what you actually meant.
Computing should be something we build together
But Personal Computing 2.0 isn’t only about a more powerful relationship between an individual and their computer. More importantly, personal Computing 2.0 is about other people and our relationships.
It’s about creating and sharing these new ways of computing and relating and exploring information. It’s about building and dreaming and collaborating together. It’s about re-thinking the past 20 years of computing and asking: what if our software worked exactly like we wanted it to?
One of my fundamental beliefs is in the innate goodness of most people. I believe that when people are healthy and happy and left to their own devices, they mostly try to help others. Most of us don’t take joy from the suffering of others, nor do we care about accumulating infinite power. We mostly want to love and be loved, to find joy where we can, to offer kindness and compassion, and to leave the world a little better than we found it.
Personal Computing 2.0 is about using our data and our computers to seize back some of the power that Big Tech has acquired--and squandered--for the better part of the last two decades.
It’s our data, our knowledge, and our power anyway. And there’s nothing stopping us--let’s start the 2nd Personal Computing revolution and build the world we want to see.
results.summary:
The proposed Personal Computing 2.0 paradigm seeks to shift digital power back to individual users by prioritizing data ownership, local control, and interoperability over centralized Big Tech ecosystems.

### Key Points
- Personal Computing 2.0 advocates for storing data locally rather than in the cloud to prevent vendor lock-in and subscription-based access restrictions.
- The model promotes cross-platform compatibility, allowing users to integrate various AI agents and software tools regardless of the underlying hardware or provider.
- By leveraging open-weight AI models, users can run powerful intelligence locally on personal devices like laptops or Raspberry Pis.
- The framework aims to solve modern privacy concerns by returning to the foundational principle that a user’s data should reside entirely under their own control.
- Advanced serverless computing and AI-driven interfaces are intended to make complex programming and data management accessible to non-engineers.

### Why it Matters
This shift represents a direct challenge to the current "closed" AI and SaaS-dominated landscape that has increasingly restricted user autonomy. By reclaiming data sovereignty, individuals can potentially mitigate the risks of platform dependency and foster a more creative, personalized digital environment.

results.title: The World’s Worst Predictions
results.author: Gary Arndt
results.content:
Podcast Transcript
Throughout history, experts, executives, scientists, and journalists have tried to predict what the future would look like.
Some of those predictions were insightful. Others were so spectacularly wrong that they became famous in their own right.
They dismissed revolutionary inventions, underestimated new technologies, and confidently predicted the exact opposite of what happened.
Learn more about some of the world’s worst predictions on this episode of Everything Everywhere Daily.
Predicting the future is difficult. Some people have pulled off incredibly prescient guesses about what the future would hold. Others haven’t just been wrong; they have been spectacularly wrong.
They might have overestimated or underestimated technologies or trends, or completely missed what was obvious to everyone else.
To be fair, predicting the future isn’t easy. If it were, everyone would do it. But there is a difference between wrong and spectacularly wrong, and that is the focus of this episode.
We’ll start with one of the worst predictions by someone who was otherwise quite talented, Irving Fisher.
Irving Fisher was an American economist, statistician, and Yale professor born in 1867. He became one of the most influential economists of the early 20th century, especially for his work on interest rates, inflation, capital theory, and the relationship between money and prices. His ideas helped shape what later became modern monetary economics.
Many economists, including Joseph Schumpeter, Milton Friedman, and James Tobin, considered him to be one of the greatest economists the United States has ever produced.
However, his reputation was tainted by one enormously wrong statement. On October 15, 1929, days before the stock market crashed, he said, “Stock prices have reached what looks like a permanently high plateau.”
He was speaking to the Purchasing Agents Association at its monthly dinner meeting. He also said, “Largely through the influence of the investment trust movement, the public has been waking up to the superior attraction of stocks over bonds. And I believe the operation of the investment trusts, as a whole, has acted to stabilize the stock market rather than to make its fluctuations more violent.”
Needless to say, the stock market wasn’t more stable, and it wasn’t sitting at a permanently high plateau. It wasn’t just that he was wrong; it was that he was wrong just days before things fell apart.
Speaking of bad timing, another horribly timed prediction appeared in a New York Times editorial on October 9, 1903. The editorial, titled Flying Machines Which Do Not Fly, responded to Samuel Langley’s attempt to test a flying machine just days earlier.
The editorial wrote: [It] might be assumed that the flying machine which will really fly might be evolved by the combined and continuous efforts of mathematicians and mechanicians in from one million to ten million years… No doubt the problem has attractions for those it interests, but to the ordinary man it would seem as if effort might be employed more profitably.
It turned out they didn’t need to wait ten million years or even one million. Just sixty-nine days later, the Wright Brothers conducted their first powered flight at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.
So they were off by only a factor of several million.
Lord Kelvin, who was one of the discoverers of the Laws of Thermodynamics, was wrong about a whole host of things.
He was invited to join the Aeronautical Society, which he declined, saying: “I have not the smallest molecule of faith in aerial navigation other than ballooning or of the expectation of good results from any of the trials we hear of … I would not care to be a member of the Aeronautical Society.”
When X-rays were discovered that could penetrate the human body, he said, “X-rays will prove to be a hoax.”
And not to be outdone, when radio was invented he said, “Radio has no future.” and “Wireless [telegraphy] is all very well, but I’d rather send a message by a boy on a pony!”
It should be noted he later recanted his views on radio after using it after a transatlantic voyage.
Skepticism about flying is somewhat understandable for the period, but it wasn’t the only transportation technology people doubted.
According to a 1922 biography of Henry Ford, a banker advised prospective Ford investor Horace Rackham: “The horse is here to stay, but the automobile is only a novelty—a fad.”
Rackham ignored the advice, invested $5,000, which he later sold for $12 million.
Someone who passed up a world-changing investment was William Orton, President of the Western Union Telegraph Company. Before he founded Bell Telephone, Alexander Graham Bell offered Orton the chance to buy the telephone patent for $100,000.
Orton turned him down and wrote about the telephone in an internal corporate memo saying: “The idea of installing ‘telephones’ in every city is idiotic… Why would any person want to use this ungainly and impractical device when he can send a messenger to the telegraph office and have a clear written message sent to any large city in the US? This ‘telephone’ has too many shortcomings to be seriously considered as a means of communication. The device is inherently of no value to us.”
Bell Telephone would go on to become the largest company in the United States.
Darryl F. Zanuck, the powerful head of 20th Century Fox Studios, was massively wrong when predicting the future of television. He said in 1951, “Television won’t be able to hold on to any market it captures after the first six months. People will soon get tired of staring at a plywood box every night.
Not to be outdone, Orrin E. Dunlap Jr., a writer for the New York Times, published in 1939, The problem with television is that the people must sit and keep their eyes glued on a screen; the average American family hasn’t time for it. Therefore, the showmen are convinced that for this reason, if for no other, television will never be a serious competitor of broadcasting.
Being wrong isn’t just about inventions and technology. Some people have really wiffed on cultural trends.
The Beatles manager Brian Epstein, in his 1965 memoir, recounted what happened when the Beatles tried to get signed by Decca Records. As Epstein recalled “We had coffee, and Mr. Rowe, a short plump man, said to me: “Not to mince words, Mr. Epstein, we don’t like your boys’ sound. Groups of four guitarists are on the way out.”
Likewise, in 1911, the New York Times published a review of an exhibition by the painter Pablo Picasso in Paris. They wrote: “It is to be regretted that this unquestionably talented artist… should now make his debut with a series of childish, not to say imbecile, scribbles that are no interest either as independent works of art or as steps toward achieving the complete work. They have neither material beauty nor that ‘spiritual significance’… nor merit of any other sort”
However, without a doubt, the worst predictions have been in the area of computers. Throughout the history of computing, there are example after example of people underestimating what computers could do.
In 1949, Popular Mechanics Magazine made a very tame prediction. At the time, the ENIAC computer used 18,000 vacuum tubes and weighed 30 tons. They predicted, “computers in the future may have only 1,000 vacuum tubes and perhaps weigh 1 ½ tons.”
The computing pioneer John von Neumann not only made a horribly wrong prediction in 1949, but he predicted that his own prediction would be wrong. He said, “It would appear that we have reached the limits of what it is possible to achieve with computer technology, although one should be careful with such statements, as they tend to sound pretty silly in 5 years.”
One of the oddest predictions regarding the internet came from someone who had a pivotal role to play in the creation of computer networking. Robert Metcalfe was the co-inventor of Ethernet and founded 3Com.
In the mid-1990s, he was convinced that the growth of the Internet would cause it to collapse in a spectacular fashion. He said, Almost all of the many predictions now being made about 1996 hinge on the Internet’s continuing exponential growth. But I predict the Internet, which only just recently got this section here in InfoWorld, will soon go spectacularly supernova and in 1996 catastrophically collapse.
Of course the collapse of the Internet didn’t occur in 1996, nor in any year thereafter.
Metcalfe was a good sport about being wrong. In 1997, he made a video of himself blending a piece of paper with his prediction and drinking it, so he literally ate his words.
Many people back in the 90s were skeptical of the internet. Perhaps the most famous wrong prediction came from Nobel Laureate Economist Paul Krugman, who said The growth of the Internet will slow drastically, as the flaw in ‘Metcalfe’s law’–which states that the number of potential connections in a network is proportional to the square of the number of participants–becomes apparent: most people have nothing to say to each other! By 2005 or so, it will become clear that the Internet’s impact on the economy has been no greater than the fax machine’s.
Needless to say, the impact of the Internet has been a bit greater than that of the fax machine.
One of the best-selling tech products of all time has been the iPhone, but there was a time when no one was sure if Apple could or would release such a device.
In 2006, the New York Times tech writer David Pogue wrote, Everyone’s always asking me when Apple will come out with a cellphone. My answer is, probably never. I cannot imagine Apple giving veto power to ANYONE over its software design. It just ain’t gonna happen.
Less than one year later, Steve Jobs introduced the iPhone.
Even after it was announced, many people thought it would fail. In particular, Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer thought that the iPhone would fall on its face. In April 2007, before it actually went on sale, he said, “Right now, we’re selling millions and millions and millions of phones a year. Apple is selling zero phones a year. In six months, they’ll have the most expensive phone by far in the marketplace, and let’s see how they do. But there’s no chance that the iPhone is going to get any significant market share. No chance.”
Of course, Apple isn’t immune to getting things wrong either. In 2003, Steve Jobs explained that the streaming music business model would never work. He noted, The subscription model of buying music is bankrupt. I think you could make available the Second Coming in a subscription model, and it might not be successful. If it costs you $10 a month, or over $100 a year, for a subscription fee to rent that song, that means for me to listen to my favorite song, in 10 years I paid over $1,000 in subscription fees to listen to my favorite song 10 years from now, and that just doesn’t fly with customers. They don’t want subscriptions.
Spotify became a multibillion-dollar business, proving Steve Jobs wrong.
Bad predictions are usually less interesting because someone was wrong than because they reveal how difficult it is to imagine a future that breaks sharply from the present. Experts tend to project existing technologies, habits, and markets forward, while revolutions often come from changes that make those assumptions obsolete.
The telephone, airplane, computer, Internet, and smartphone all looked limited or unnecessary to people who understood the world as it already existed.
History’s worst predictions are reminders that expertise can explain the present very well while still offering no guarantee of seeing what comes next.
results.summary:
History is filled with spectacularly incorrect predictions from experts and industry leaders who failed to foresee the transformative impact of revolutionary technologies like the telephone, internet, and smartphone.

### Key Points
- Economist Irving Fisher famously claimed stock prices had reached a "permanently high plateau" just days before the 1929 market crash.
- The New York Times predicted in 1903 that human flight would take millions of years to achieve, only for the Wright Brothers to succeed 69 days later.
- Western Union President William Orton rejected the opportunity to buy the telephone patent, calling the device "inherently of no value."
- Microsoft CEO Steve Ballmer dismissed the iPhone in 2007, claiming it had "no chance" of gaining significant market share.
- Apple co-founder Steve Jobs incorrectly predicted that the music subscription business model would fail, despite the later success of services like Spotify.
- Ethernet co-inventor Robert Metcalfe predicted the internet would catastrophically collapse in 1996, later famously eating his printed prediction after being proven wrong.

### Why it Matters
These historical miscalculations demonstrate that even highly credentialed experts often struggle to envision futures that deviate from existing habits and market structures. Understanding these failures highlights the inherent difficulty in predicting disruptive innovation and serves as a cautionary tale for relying solely on current trends to forecast long-term progress.
